[2] H-MEM: Hierarchical Memory for High-Efficiency
[3] Long-Term Reasoning in LLM Agents
[4] Haoran Sun, Shaoning Zeng
[5] Abstract
[6] Long-term memory is one of the key factors
[7] influencing the reasoning capabilities of Large
[8] Language Model Agents (LLM Agents). In-
[9] corporating a memory mechanism that effec-
[10] tively integrates past interactions can signifi-
[11] cantly enhance decision-making and contex-
[12] tual coherence of LLM Agents. While recent
[13] works have made progress in memory storage
[14] and retrieval, such as encoding memory into
[15] dense vectors for similarity-based search or
[16] organizing knowledge in the form of graph,
[17] these approaches often fall short in structured
[18] memory organization and efficient retrieval. To
[19] address these limitations, we propose a Hier-
[20] archical Memory (H-MEM) architecture for
[21] LLM Agents that organizes and updates mem-
[22] ory in a multi-level fashion based on the de-
[23] gree of semantic abstraction. Each memory
[24] vector is embedded with a positional index en-
[25] coding pointing to its semantically related sub-
[26] memories in the next layer. During the reason-
[27] ing phase, an index-based routing mechanism
[28] enables efficient, layer-by-layer retrieval with-
[29] out performing exhaustive similarity computa-
[30] tions. We evaluate our method on five task set-
[31] tings from the LoCoMo dataset. Experimental
[32] results show that our approach consistently out-
[33] performs five baseline methods, demonstrating
[34] its effectiveness in long-term dialogue scenar-
[35] ios.
[36] 1 Introduction
[37] Large Language Models (LLM) Agents possess
[38] the capability to autonomously make decisions and
[39] perform a wide range of tasks, with particularly
[40] strong performance in question-answering scenar-
[41] ios (Huang et al., 2024a; Yao et al., 2024). In long-
[42] term conversational settings, the decision-making
[43] and reasoning processes of LLM Agents often re-
[44] quire integrating historical interactions, thereby
[45] relying heavily on their internal memory mech-
[46] anisms (Li et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). The

[55] namic nature of human-like cognitive memory by
[56] retaining prior dialogue information (Shen, 2024).
[57] This allows the model to effectively retrieve rele-
[58] vant memory content during response generation,
[59] enabling context-aware and personalized replies
[60] (Zhang et al., 2024a). The effective design of mem-
[61] ory mechanisms plays a critical role in enhancing
[62] the performance of LLM Agents in complex and
[63] extended dialogue tasks (Wu et al., 2025).
[64] The most basic memory mechanism involves
[65] simple multi-turn dialogue, where all previous in-
[66] teractions with LLM are concatenated with the cur-
[67] rent prompt and user query (Huang et al., 2024b; Yi
[68] et al., 2024). However, this approach is limited by
[69] the context window length of LLMs, making it in-
[70] effective for long-term interactions. This limitation
[71] has promoted researchers to explore more efficient
[72] memory mechanisms. MemGPT adopts a layered
[73] memory architecture inspired by operating systems,
[74] combining a limited context window with external
[75] storage (Packer et al., 2023). However, its external

[79] memory design relies on retrieval-augmented mod-
[80] els, which may face trade-offs between retrieval ac-
[81] curacy and response efficiency when dealing with
[82] large-scale information. MemInsight strengthens
[83] the memory representation of LLM agents by au-
[84] tonomously extracting key information and gen-
[85] erating structured attributes (Salama et al., 2025).
[86] A-MEM, inspired by the Zettelkasten method, im-
[87] plements a self-organizing and evolving memory
[88] system by dynamically constructing a network of
[89] knowledge (Xu et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the com-
[90] plexity of such memory structures introduces con-
[91] sistency and accuracy challenges in maintaining
[92] and updating inter-node relationships. Memory-
[93] Bank enhances long-term interaction capabilities
[94] by encoding memories into vector representations
[95] and retrieving them through similarity-based search
[96] (Zhong et al., 2024). This vector-based encoding
[97] approach improves the efficiency of both memory
[98] storage and retrieval (Zhang et al., 2024a). Never-
[99] theless, as the number of memory entries increases,
[100] the computational complexity of vector retrieval
[101] also rises sharply, posing challenges to system per-
[102] formance.
[103] In order to optimize the ability of existing mem-
[104] ory mechanisms in structured storage, systematic
[105] organization, and efficient retrieval, we propose a
[106] novel Hierarchical Memory (H-MEM) architecture.
[107] H-MEM adopts a hierarchical memory structure,
[108] dividing memory into four levels according to the
[109] degree of semantic abstraction, corresponding to
[110] structures similar to section, subsection, subsub-
[111] section, and content. In this structure, the memory
[112] vectors of each level are embedded in the position
[113] index encoding of their subordinate sub-memories,
[114] which enables efficient screening of relevant mem-
[115] ory units through upper-level semantic information
[116] during the retrieval process, and then continues to
[117] retrieve the corresponding related sub-memories of
[118] the next layer based on the relevant memories. As
[119] shown in Figure 1, H-MEM not only enhances the
[120] organization and structure of memory retrieval, but
[121] also significantly reduces the participation range of
[122] irrelevant information, thereby effectively reducing
[123] computational costs and achieving efficient and tar-
[124] geted memory access. Our main contributions are
[125] summarized as follows.
[126] • H-MEM, a hierarchical memory architecture
[127] for LLM agents, is proposed to integrate multi-
[128] level memory storage with positional index en-
[129] coding of sub-memory at each layer, enabling
[130] structured and systematic memory organiza-
[131] tion as well as efficient and orderly memory
[132] retrieval. In addition, we design a more sci-
[133] entific memory update mechanism to adapt
[134] to the complex psychological changes of hu-
[135] mans.
[136] • We compare H-MEM with five baseline meth-
[137] ods across multiple large language models on
[138] five question-answering tasks from the Lo-
[139] CoMo dataset. Experimental results demon-
[140] strate the effectiveness of H-MEM in optimiz-
[141] ing memory storage structures and the effi-
[142] ciency of memory retrieval.
[143] 2 Related Work
[144] 2.1 Memory for LLM Agents
[145] To enhance the long-term reasoning capabilities
[146] of LLM Agents, numerous researchers have ex-
[147] plored memory mechanisms of it (Zhang et al.,
[148] 2024b; Huang et al., 2024a; Hatalis et al., 2023).
[149] ReadAgent is an LLM-based agent system that
[150] significantly extends the effective context length
[151] of LLMs and improves reading comprehension
[152] by segmenting long texts into pages, compress-
[153] ing them into key-point memories, and perform-
[154] ing interactive retrieval when needed (Lee et al.,
[155] 2024). MemGPT leverages a virtual context man-
[156] agement technique to extend the context window
[157] of LLMs (Packer et al., 2023). It adopts a layered
[158] memory architecture similar to that of an operating
[159] system, integrating limited internal context with
[160] external storage. Through function calls, it dynam-
[161] ically manages data, allowing effective process-
[162] ing of long documents and multi-turn dialogues
[163] (Zhang et al., 2024b). The Self-Controlled Mem-
[164] ory (SCM) framework strengthens LLMs’ ability
[165] to handle long texts and long-term memory via
[166] three core components: the LLM agent, memory
[167] stream, and memory controller (Wang et al., 2023).
[168] SCM dynamically determines when and how to uti-
[169] lize memory, improving information retrieval and
[170] response quality. A-MEM, inspired by the Zettelka-
[171] sten method, is a memory system for LLM agents
[172] that enables self-organizing and evolving memory
[173] through the dynamic construction of a knowledge
[174] network. It creates structured memory notes for
[175] new entries and establishes connections with histor-
[176] ical memories through contextual analysis. As new
[177] memories are added, the system updates contex-
[178] tual representations of existing ones, progressively

[203] ing, and more personalized and natural interactions
[204] (Zhong et al., 2024). While this method solves

[206] well, there are still shortcomings in structured mem-
[207] ory storage and efficient systematic memory re-

[210] 3 Method
[211] 3.1 Memory Storage
[212] The storage layer of H-MEM is organized into a
[213] four-level hierarchical structure, designed accord-
[214] ing to increasing levels of semantic abstraction and
[215] generalization. As shown in Figure 2, from top to
[216] bottom, these layers are: Domain Layer, Category
[217] Layer, Memory Trace Layer, and Episode Layer.
[218] This hierarchy resembles the structure of a doc-
[219] ument, analogous to section, subsection, subsub-
[220] section, and content, respectively. The first three
[221] layers serve as a progressively refined index, pro-
[222] viding a systematic and interpretable organization
[223] of memory, while the bottom layer contains the
[224] actual episodic content and user profile informa-
[225] tion. The approximate simplified meaning of the
[226] prompt is: "You are a information analyze agent
[227] for a long-term LLM system. Given a dialogue, you
[228] must extract and structure the information into a
[229] hierarchical memory format. Follow this hierarchy
[230] strictly: 1. Identify the high-level domain of inter-
[231] est. 2. Extract specific categories or subdomains
[232] related to the topic. 3. Summarize the keywords of
[233] the dialogue. 4. Extract specific events and user
[234] profile. Output the result as structured JSON. ".
[235] After each interaction between the user and the
[236] large language model (LLM), a specialized mem-
[237] ory extraction model is invoked to analyze the in-
[238] teraction and extract multi-level structured infor-
[239] mation. Guided by carefully designed prompts,
[240] this model parses the interaction into four seman-
[241] tic layers. For example, when a user requests a
[242] recommendation for an action movie or a skiing
[243] 
[244] === Page 4 ===
[245] competition, the LLM might suggest a Kung Fu
[246] movie starring Jackie Chan and a competition fea-
[247] turing Mikaela Shiffrin. The first three layers store
[248] abstract summaries similar to directories. Episode
[249] Layer stores the complete contextual memory of
[250] the interaction, including a timestamp and an in-
[251] ferred user profile. This profile reflects the user’s
[252] preferences, interests, emotional states, and behav-
[253] ioral patterns. All memory entries are encoded
[254] into dense vector representations using a neural en-
[255] coder to support efficient semantic retrieval. The
[256] structured design of H-MEM enhances the inter-
[257] pretability of stored information while ensuring
[258] scalability for memory retrieval in long-term inter-
[259] actions, thus enabling more fine-grained reasoning.
[260] In the Episode Layer, both vector representations
[261] and textual memory are preserved: the vectors are
[262] used for similarity computation, while the text is
[263] used to select the final memory content, which is
[264] then integrated with prompts to provide accurate
[265] memory grounding for the LLM.
[266] We also designed a self-adaptation hierarchy ad-
[267] justment interface, allowing users to dynamically
[268] adjust the hierarchy structure based on the com-
[269] plexity of the current conversation and the semantic
[270] granularity of the memorized content. For exam-
[271] ple, in simple conversations, the number of levels
[272] can be reduced to improve efficiency; while in con-
[273] versations involving multiple topics and complex
[274] relationships, levels can be added to better organize
[275] memory.

[380] 3.3 Memory Update
[381] Existing research has effectively simulated the for-
[382] getting process of human memory with the help of
[383] the Ebbinghaus Forgetting Curve, taking into ac-
[384] count the characteristics of the enhanced strength
[385] of memory after it is called upon (Zhong et al.,
[386] 2024). However, such methods ignore the dynamic
[387] changes in human psychological states. In fact, hu-
[388] man interests and behavioral preferences are com-
[389] plex and changeable. For example, a user may have
[390] been enthusiastic about skiing before, but after a
[391] period of time, due to the influence of some inter-
[392] mediate events, they developed a strong aversion to
[393] skiing. To more realistically model the variability
[394] of human memory, we introduce a dynamic mem-
[395] ory regulation mechanism based on LLM based
[396] on user feedback on the basis of traditional forget-
[397] ting curves. Specifically, when LLM calls a certain
[398] memory to generate an answer, H-MEM will adjust
[399] the weight of the corresponding memory based on
[400] the feedback performance (approval, no obvious
[401] feedback, or rebuttal) of user: if the user shows
[402] approval, the weight of the memory will be en-
[403] hanced, which is regarded as the reinforcement of
[404] effective memory; if there is no feedback, it will
[405] follow the original forgetting curve Natural Shrink;
[406] if the user refutes, the weight of the memory will
[407] be reduced, indicating that the memory may have
[408] expired. The above enhancement or weakening
[409] process is updated by multiplying with the feed-
[410] back weight generated by LLM, thereby achieving
[411] dynamic adjustment of memory strength.
[412] 4 Experiment
[413] 4.1 Setup
[414] Datasets. To evaluate the effectiveness of H-MEM
[415] in long-term dialogue settings, we adopted the
[416] LoCoMo dataset following established practices.
[417] LoCoMo dataset is specifically designed to
[418] assess the memory capabilities of large language
[419] model (LLM) agents in extended multi-session
[420] interactions. It comprises 50 dialogues, each
[421] averaging 300 turns and spanning up to 35 sessions,
[422] with an average of 9,000 tokens per dialogue.
[423] The dataset includes 7,512 question-answer
[424] pairs categorized into five types: (1) single-hop
[425] questions answerable from a single session (SH.)-
[426] 2705 pairs; (2) multi-hop questions requiring
[427] information synthesis across sessions (MH.)-
[428] 1104 pairs; (3) temporal reasoning questions
[429] testing understanding of time-related information
[430] (T.)- 1547 pairs; (4) open-domain knowledge
[431] questions requiring integration of conversation
[432] context with external knowledge (OD.)- 285
[433] pairs; and (5) adversarial questions assessing
[434] models’ ability to identify unanswerable queries
[435] (A.)- 1871 pairs. LoCoMo ensures long-range
[436] consistency across entire dialogues, making it
[437] well-suited for evaluating a LLM’s ability to
[438] handle long-distance dependencies and maintain
[439] coherence over extended conversations.
[440] Implementation Details. We conduct experi-
[441] ments using Qwen-1.5B/3B (Yang et al., 2024a),
[442] LLaMA 3.2-1B/3B (Touvron et al., 2023), and
[443] DeepSeek-R1 1.5B/7B (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) as
[444] the base question-answering models. BERT is
[445] employed as the encoder for memory storage. For
[446] similarity computation, we utilize FAISS (Douze
[447] et al., 2024) and retrieve the top-k memories with
[448]

[450] k = 10. Regarding the baselines, we follow the
[451] original papers in terms of experimental data and
[452] configuration settings (Packer et al., 2023; Zhong
[453] et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025). DeepSeek-R1-8B
[454] (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) is primarily used for memory
[455] analysis and information extraction. To eliminate
[456] the influence of model type, we also include
[457] Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2024b) and LLaMA
[458] 3.2-3B (Touvron et al., 2023) in ablation studies.
[459] All models used in our experiments are deployed
[460] locally via Ollama on a system equipped with two
[461] NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs.
[462] Baselines. In the experiments, we compare our
[463] work on the five types of tasks with other long-term
[464] memory methods of LLM. These methods include
[465] LoCoMo (LCM.) (Maharana et al., 2024), ReadA-
[466] gent (RA.) (Lee et al., 2024), MemoryBank (MB.)
[467] (Zhong et al., 2024), MemGPT (MG.) (Packer
[468] et al., 2023), and A-MEM (AM.) (Xu et al., 2025).
[469] Among them, the LoCoMo method is the original
[470] evaluation method of the LoCoMo dataset itself,
[471] similar to the general multi-round dialogue, with-
[472] out using special memory mechanisms, directly
[473] using the basic model for question answering tasks.
[474] Before each interaction, the complete previous
[475] historical interaction information is combined with
[476] the question and prompt.
[477] Evaluation Metrics. We utilize two primary
[478] metrics to comprehensively assess the performance
[479] of the LLM equipped with different memory. The
[480] F1 score is employed to evaluate the accuracy of
[481] the answers by calculating the harmonic mean of
[482] precision and recall, thereby providing a balanced
[483] measure of the model’s ability to generate both
[484] relevant and complete responses. The BLEU-1
[485] score is used to assess the quality of the generated
[486] responses by measuring word overlap with ground
[487] truth responses between the output of LLM, which
[488] helps in evaluating the lexical precision of the
[489] generated text.
[490] Computational Efficiency Experiment Design.
[491] In addition to the effectiveness evaluation exper-
[492] iments described earlier, we designed a Compu-
[493] tational Efficiency Analysis experiment to assess
[494] the memory retrieval efficiency of H-MEM in a
[495] continuous reasoning scenario with huge amount
[496] of irrelevant memories. In this setting, five task
[497] types—Single Hop, Multi Hop, Temporal, Open
[498] Domain, and Adversarial—are executed sequen-
[499] tially as a single run. During the process, the stored
[500] memory is not cleared between task switches but is
[501] continuously accumulated. This design simulates
[502] real-world usage and aims to evaluate whether H-
[503] MEM can maintain efficient memory retrieval as
[504] the volume of stored memory increases. Among
[505] all the baseline methods, only MemoryBank and
[506] H-MEM adopt a memory mechanism that encodes
[507] memory into vector representations and retrieves
[508] it via similarity-based matching. Therefore, we
[509] conduct the efficiency comparison solely between
[510] H-MEM and MemoryBank. In this experiment, we
[511] use BERT as the encoder, employ Flat of FAISS
[512] for similarity-based retrieval, and set the top-k pa-
[513] rameter to k=10. The base model for the tasks is
[514] Qwen-1.5B, while the memory reasoning module
[515] is implemented using DeepSeek-R1-8B.
[516] 4.2 Results and Analysis
[517] Comparison to Baselines. As shown in the
[518] Table 1, we conducted systematic comparative
[519] experiments on five categories of tasks from the
[520] LoCoMo dataset, evaluating five mainstream
[521] baseline methods across multiple large language
[522] models (LLMs) of varying scales. This comprehen-
[523] sive evaluation aims to assess the effectiveness and
[524] stability of H-MEM in long-term dialogue tasks.
[525] Overall, our method consistently achieves the
[526] highest average F1 and BLEU-1 scores across all
[527] model and task configurations, with improvements
[528] of 14.98 and 12.77 points over the baselines,
[529] respectively, demonstrating its generalizability and
[530] significant advantages. In relatively basic tasks
[531] such as Single-Hop, Temporal, and Open-Domain
[532] dialogue, H-MEM consistently outperforms all
[533] baselines, providing preliminary evidence of its
[534] effectiveness in long-term dialogue modeling.
[535] More notably, in more challenging tasks such as
